what: The ROI Calculator measures how much you gained or lost on an investment, as a percentage of what you put in, and turns it into a yearly figure so different investments can be compared fairly.
A second tab finds the break-even point for a product or small business: how many units you must sell before fixed costs are covered and profit begins. A chart shows where sales overtake costs.
uses: See which property, shares or business gave the best yearly return.
Compare what a campaign cost with the profit it brought in.
Find how many units you need to sell at different prices.
Know your break-even before you buy stock or equipment.
Add a target profit to see the units you need.
tutorial: Tap Return on investment or Break-even.
Type the amount invested, the final value or amount returned (including any income it paid) and any extra costs such as fees or repairs.
Type how long you held it and choose years, months or days to get the yearly (annualized) ROI.
Type fixed costs, the selling price per unit and the variable cost per unit.
Type a profit you want to see how many units it takes.
Check the results and the chart, then press Copy result.
features: Total and yearly return in one place.
Include fees and repairs for an honest ROI.
Units needed for the profit you want.
Sales and total cost lines show where profit starts.
About 40 currencies or your own symbol.

example.title: Worked example: 10,000 that became 13,500 in 3 years
example.text: The gain is 3,500, so ROI = 3,500 ÷ 10,000 = 35%. The annualized ROI is (13,500 ÷ 10,000)^(1/3) − 1 = 10.52% a year. For break-even: fixed costs 5,000, price 25 and variable cost 10 give a margin of 15 per unit, so you need 5,000 ÷ 15 = 333.3, rounded up to 334 units (8,350 in sales).

tips: Always add fees, taxes and repairs to the cost for a true ROI.
Compare investments by yearly ROI, not total ROI, when they last different lengths of time.
Very short holding periods make yearly ROI look extreme; treat it with care.
Lowering variable costs often moves break-even more than raising prices.
problems: The amount invested must be above 0.
The period is very short compared with the gain. Use a longer period or rely on total ROI.
The price must be higher than the variable cost per unit.
